DNA Motif Finder: Comparing KMP and Rabin–Karp 
Har Agam Deep Singh  |  03714802724  |  Section 5C123 
Submitted to Dr. Jyoti Kaushik 
DAA · Assignment 4 · CIC-311 · 17 November 2026 
1. Abstract 
This project implements an exact DNA motif finder using Knuth –Morris–Pratt (KMP) and Rabin–Karp string matching. Both 
algorithms locate every occurrence of a given motif, including overlaps. A Python command -line application validates 
inputs and exports match positions. Experiments compare execution time and character comparisons on five DNA lengths 
using random and repetitive sequences. A separate experiment varies the hash modulus to measure spurious hits. The 
saved run contains 525 timing samples. KMP is faster in the measured comparisons, while larger moduli reduce Rabin –
Karp collisions. Correctness is established through oracle comparisons, edge cases, and deliberate collision tests.  
2. Problem statement and objectives 
Given a DNA sequence T of length n and a nonempty motif P of length m over {A, C, G, T}, return all indices i for which 
T[i:i+m] = P. Indices are zero-based. The assignment requires at least two algorithms for the same problem, complexity 
analysis, measured comparisons on at least five input sizes, and a study of spurious hits versus modulus q [1].  
The objectives are to implement both algorithms transparently, verify identical outputs, separate character comparisons 
from hash work, measure reproducible timing trends, and explain how input repetition and modulus choice affect 
performance. The selected pair is KMP and Rabin–Karp. 
Input DNA Motif Expected positions 
ACGTACGTGACG ACG 0, 4, 9 
AAAAA AAA 0, 1, 2 (overlapping) 
3. System workflow and scope 
 
Figure 1. Application workflow; both algorithms receive the same normalized DNA and motif. 
This is an exact single-pattern search tool, not a biological motif-discovery model. It accepts plain text DNA, normalizes 
case and whitespace, and rejects ambiguous symbols such as N, FASTA headers, and empty motifs. Empty DNA or m > n 
produces an empty match list. The console previews up to 20 positions; JSON export retains every match.

4. Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP) 
KMP avoids restarting the pattern at each mismatch. It first builds an LPS array, where LPS[i] is the length of the longest 
proper prefix of P[0:i+1] that is also a suffix. A proper prefix excludes the whole substring. During search, j is the number  of 
currently matched pattern characters; LPS determines how much of that work can be reused.  
Index i 0 1 2 3 4 5 
P[i] A C A C A G 
LPS[i] 0 0 1 2 3 0 
 
Figure 2. In ACACA, prefix ACA equals suffix ACA. After a mismatch at j = 5, reuse 3 characters. 
For P = ACACAG, a mismatch after ACACA falls back from j = 5 to LPS[4] = 3. The text position does not move backward. 
The next comparison uses P[3]. Further mismatches may cause additional LPS fallbacks. After a full match, j becomes 
LPS[m−1], preserving overlapping occurrences. 
4.1 Pseudocode 
BUILD_LPS(P): 
    LPS ← array of m zeros; length ← 0; i ← 1 
    while i < m: 
        if P[i] = P[length]: 
            length ← length + 1; LPS[i] ← length; i ← i + 1 
        else if length > 0: length ← LPS[length − 1] 
        else: i ← i + 1 
    return LPS 
 
KMP(T, P): 
    reject empty P; if m > n: return [] 
    LPS ← BUILD_LPS(P); i ← 0; j ← 0; matches ← [] 
    while i < n: 
        if T[i] = P[j]: 
            i ← i + 1; j ← j + 1 
            if j = m: 
                append i − m to matches; j ← LPS[j − 1] 
        else if j > 0: j ← LPS[j − 1] 
        else: i ← i + 1 
    return matches 
4.2 Correctness and complexity 
Before each search comparison, the first j motif characters equal the text suffix ending immediately before i. A successful 
comparison extends this invariant. On failure, an LPS fallback retains a prefix already known to match that suffix. Shorter 
candidate borders remain available, so no valid occurrence is skipped. When j = m, the reported index i−m is therefore a 
complete match. 
LPS construction takes O(m) time. During search, i only advances, and decreases of j are bounded by its preceding 
increases; total search work is O(n). Overall time is O(n+m), with O(m) auxiliary space for LPS. Storing k returned positions  
adds O(k) output space. Preprocessing and search character comparisons are recorded separately.

5. Rabin–Karp rolling-hash matching 
Rabin–Karp compares numeric hashes before checking characters. Encode A=0, C=1, G=2, T=3, use base b=4, and reduce 
modulo q > 1. A window hash is h(S) = (Σ code(S[j]) × 4^(m−1−j)) mod q. Equal hashes are candidates, not proof of equal 
strings. Every candidate is verified character by character, stopping at the first mismatch.  
high = 4^(m−1) mod q 
next_hash = (4 × (window_hash − code(T[i]) × high) + code(T[i+m])) mod q  
 
Figure 3. Rolling from ACG to CGT and a separate deliberate collision example. Hash equality requires verification. 
5.1 Pseudocode 
RABIN_KARP(T, P, q): 
    reject empty P or invalid q; if m > n: return [] 
    high ← 4^(m−1) mod q; pHash ← 0; tHash ← 0 
    for j ← 0 to m−1: 
        pHash ← (4 × pHash + code(P[j])) mod q 
        tHash ← (4 × tHash + code(T[j])) mod q 
    matches ← [] 
    for i ← 0 to n−m: 
        count one hash check 
        if pHash = tHash: 
            count one hash hit; matched ← true 
            for j ← 0 to m−1: 
                count one verification character comparison 
                if T[i+j] ≠ P[j]: matched ← false; break 
            if matched: append i to matches 
            else: count one spurious hit 
        if i < n−m: update tHash with the rolling formula 
    return matches 
5.2 Correctness, spurious hits, and complexity 
The initial hash represents the first window. Subtracting the outgoing weighted character, multiplying by 4, and appending 
the incoming code preserves that representation for each successive window. Every actual match has the motif hash and 
passes verification. A collision is rejected, so changing q affects candidate work but cannot introduce a false reported 
match. 
A spurious hit is a hash-equal window whose characters differ from the motif. Thus hash hits = true matches + spurious 
hits. If H windows have equal hashes, preprocessing plus search costs O(n+m+Hm) as an upper bound. With few 
verifications this is typically O(n+m); the worst case is O(nm). Even genuine matches can cause worst -case verification 
work. 
Property KMP Rabin–Karp 
Preprocessing O(m) O(m) 
Worst-case total time O(n+m) O(nm) 
Auxiliary space O(m) O(1) 
Extra output space O(k) O(k) 
Table 1. Complexity assumes fixed-size modulus arithmetic and excludes input storage. Both methods include overlapping 
matches.

6. Implementation and experimental method 
The implementation uses Python 3.14.0 (CPython) on Windows 11, with Matplotlib 3.10.8 for graphs. The recorded 
processor is Intel64 Family 6 Model 170 Stepping 4, with 22 logical CPUs. Source and dataset SHA -256 hashes are saved 
with the results so the measured implementation can be identified. 
Component Responsibility 
src/algorithms.py LPS, KMP, Rabin–Karp, normalization, optional metrics 
src/main.py File input, algorithm selection, validation, JSON export 
src/benchmark.py Deterministic datasets, timing batches, CSV and metadata 
src/plot_results.py; src/verify_results.py Measured graphs/tables and independent result audit 
Five lengths are tested: 1,000, 5,000, 10,000, 50,000, and 100,000 characters. Motif length is fixed at m=12, with seeds 42, 
43, and 44. Random DNA is generated uniformly and a motif is planted halfway through; incidental matches are also 
counted. Repetitive DNA consists of one repeated base and has n−m+1 overlapping matches. Both algorithms receive 
identical inputs; the scaling experiment uses q=1009. 
Each input uses two warmups, one calibration, and seven timed repetitions. Batches target 5 ms and are capped at 100 
searches; elapsed batch time is divided by the batch count. Algorithm order reverses on alternate repetitions. 
time.perf_counter_ns() measures durations [2]. Timings include preprocessing, search, and output -list construction, but 
exclude validation, generation, I/O, and metric increments. Character counts are collected in a separate instrumented 
pass. 
Each CSV timing summary is a median of seven repetitions. Tables and graphs below use the median of the three seed 
medians; runtime error bars show their minimum and maximum, not confidence intervals. There are 60 scaling rows and 
15 collision rows, giving 525 saved repetition timings in total.

Figure 4. Runtime versus DNA length. Error bars show the range of seed medians; axes differ between datasets. 
KMP is faster in all ten dataset/size comparisons in this run. At n=100,000 on random DNA, the medians are 8.5972 ms for 
KMP and 19.6482 ms for Rabin–Karp. Repetitive inputs require many candidate verifications and output positions. These 
observations describe this Python implementation and machine, not a universal algorithm ranking.

8. Character comparisons and modulus experiment 
KMP comparisons include LPS construction and text/pattern checks. Rabin –Karp character comparisons count only 
candidate verification; hash equality checks and rolling arithmetic are separate work. A smaller character count therefore 
does not necessarily imply a shorter runtime. 
 
Figure 5. Median character comparisons across seeds. Logarithmic vertical axes keep the small Rabin–Karp random-input counts 
visible. 
At n=100,000 KMP comparisons RK comparisons True matches 
Random DNA 124,721 141 1 (median) 
Repetitive DNA 100,011 1,199,868 99,989 
Table 3. Total character comparisons and match counts. In repetitive DNA, Rabin–Karp verifies all 12 characters in each of 99,989 
windows. 
For the modulus experiment, n=100,000 and m=12 remain fixed. Each seed uses the same random DNA/motif pair for all 
five q values; base and encoding also remain fixed. The results isolate the effect of the modulus on hash collisions. Every 
modulus produces the same true match positions. 
 
Figure 6. Median spurious hits versus q; both axes are logarithmic. Bars show minimum/maximum counts across seeds.  
Modulus q Median spurious hits Minimum Maximum 
5 20,051 19,785 20,151 
11 9,102 9,067 9,216 
101 995 965 1,009 
1009 96 94 99 
10007 12 11 12 
Table 4. Collision counts over 99,989 windows per seed. The median true-match count is one for every q. 
Median spurious hits decrease from 20,051 at q=5 to 12 at q=10007. This agrees with the expectation that a larger hash 
range often reduces random collisions. It is not a guarantee of strict monotonic improvement for arbitrary strings. 
Character verification is essential at every modulus, as the AA/CC example demonstrates.

9. Correctness and validation 
Nine automated test methods pass. They compare both algorithms with a separate brute -force oracle on all strings over 
{A,C} through length five and motifs of lengths one to three, plus 300 seeded random pairs. The tests check overlapping 
and boundary matches, no matches, a single-character motif, equal text/motif, empty DNA, and a motif longer than its 
text. 
Additional checks validate LPS values and hand-counted comparisons, reject empty motifs and invalid symbols, and 
confirm that the deliberate modulo-5 AA/CC collision is not reported as a match. CLI tests cover selection of either 
algorithm, invalid q, missing files, normalized input, and full JSON exports beyond the 20 -position console preview. 
Every benchmark input also agrees with an independent repeated built -in string-search reference. The saved-result audit 
reconstructs datasets, recomputes metrics, checks hash-hit identities, reconciles timing medians with all 525 raw samples, 
and verifies that plotted aggregates match the CSV data. SHA-256 checks connect the saved run to its source files and 
generated inputs. 
10. Discussion and limitations 
The random-input results illustrate a distinction between counting character comparisons and measuring total work: 
Rabin–Karp makes far fewer character checks, but performs modular arithmetic and dictionary lookups at each window. 
KMP avoids that hash work and is faster here. On repetitive DNA, KMP reuses matched structure; Rabin –Karp verifies 
every true match, causing 12 checks per window. 
With fixed m=12, even O(nm) work can appear approximately linear as n increases. This experiment does not establish 
empirical scaling in m. Some timings are not proportional to input size, particularly for smaller repetitive inputs. 
Scheduling, CPU state, allocation, or background activity may contribute; the experiment does not isolate their causes. 
Reversing algorithm order and retaining raw repetitions helps make the comparison inspectable, but does not remove all 
timing noise. 
The evidence is limited to synthetic strings, three seeds, one motif length, and one machine. Repetitive seeds can choose 
the same base, so they do not represent three independent workload types. The tool supports exact A/C/G/T matching 
only; it does not handle ambiguous bases, substitutions, insertions, deletions, or biological significance.  
11. Conclusion and future work 
Both algorithms correctly find all exact motif positions, including overlaps. KMP provides O(n+m) worst -case time and 
stable reuse of repeated structure. Rabin–Karp demonstrates rolling hashes and the importance of collision verification; 
larger moduli reduce spurious hits in the measured inputs. KMP is faster in this saved run, while the collision experiment 
explains how q changes Rabin–Karp verification work. Future work can vary motif length, add finite -automaton matching, 
and support validated FASTA input or approximate matching as separate extensions. 
12. Reproduction and submission contents 
python -m src.main data/example.txt ACG 
python -m tests.run_checks 
python -m src.benchmark 
python -m src.plot_results

Run commands from the project root after installing requirements.txt. Submit this report together with src/, tests/, data/, 
requirements.txt, and README.md. Supporting measurements are in results/; original graphs are in figures/. The sample 
command returns positions [0, 4, 9]. Benchmark timings will vary on rerun; the generated sequences and correctness 
outcomes are deterministic.
